answers.text: Every driver's text reads a bit differently, so I would say: reply with exactly three lines every time, same order — drop-off time, pallet count, then any damage noted. That way the log entry looks the same whatever the message said.

For the call log, I would say: list each entry with time, customer, topic, outcome, in that order, and then count up how many have 'needs follow-up' as the outcome so the total always comes from the list itself, not someone's memory.

The timing does not work — access from 8am plus six hours on-site should finish early afternoon on the 22nd itself, the same day, not the 23rd like the note says. That is a full day out from what the numbers actually add up to.
118 compared with 96 is not really a 20% rise — that works out closer to 23%, so that is the one I would flag. The on-time rate and the balance split both looked fine to me on a quick check.
I would sign off Output 2, since it shows the actual ticket numbers, 827 out of 940, rather than just the 88% figure. Output 1 does not tell you where the number comes from.
I would go with Email 2, since it has the actual numbers in it.
1. No, keep the pricing internal. 2. Yes, just a total. 3. No, not signed off. 4. Yes, it is already published on their site, so no harm pasting that one in. 5. No, that is someone's home address.

The hourly rates and retainer cap I would treat with care, same with the non-disclosure clause since it names both companies. I am not sure about the rest so I would probably hold all of it back rather than guess.
Before it goes to the manager at month end, I would check the closing stock count against the warehouse system as a set step in the process.

Step 1 carries some risk, since a misread invoice number would carry through everything after it. But step 4 is the one that worries me more — once the payment note is submitted automatically, that is money moving, so that is where I would want a check before it goes.
